---
name: solution-exploration
description: "Explore solutions to a product or architecture problem before consulting existing ADRs, then assess decision impacts. Use on /solution-exploration, a proposed new direction, or a reported limit of the current design. For initial architecture authoring, use /architect."
---

# Explore solutions without anchoring on past decisions

Work in two passes. Keep the first pass independent of existing ADRs, even when
the user names a current decision. An `Accepted` ADR describes what is in force;
its status is not evidence that the choice still serves the problem best.

## 1. Explore from the problem

Clarify the outcome, product needs, constraints and decision criteria. Inspect
relevant code, behavior and other evidence as needed, but **do not read or use
`docs/adr/` or the decision log and ADR-summary portions of
`docs/ARCHITECTURE.md` in this pass**. Other product and architecture evidence
may be read. Develop credible options, including the user's
proposal and keeping the current design when relevant. Give each option its
strongest case, costs, risks and unknowns. Form a provisional recommendation from
this comparison; say what evidence could change it. A request to consider a new
project or direction deserves a genuine assessment, without presuming the current
path will win. Make the provisional recommendation observable in an interim reply
or a scratch note before opening any decision record; do not silently replace it.

## 2. Reconcile with the decision record

Only after the provisional recommendation is visible, read the project's decision
rule if installed (`agent/decisions.md`) and the relevant ADRs. The workflow and
human status boundary here still apply when the `agent` module is not installed.
Follow dependent ADRs when an option
changes their assumptions or invariants; a shared authorization model, for
example, can affect many decisions. Classify records by their explicit status
line, including `Rejected`, `Rejeté`, or `Refusé`; do not infer status from a title.
Search for relevant rejected records and alternatives refused inside accepted
ADRs. Identify the exact proposal and why it was refused. Compare the new option
with that proposal: is it the same solution, or materially
different? Test whether the old objections still hold under current constraints
and evidence, and say what would justify reopening the choice. A past refusal is
neither a permanent veto nor disposable history.

Compare the options against decisions in force, original rationale, current
evidence, migration costs, and conflicts that would require new human
arbitration. Do not reopen unrelated records. Revise the recommendation if the
ADRs reveal a real constraint or cost; explain any change from the first pass.
Never reject an option solely because an ADR is `Accepted`.

Hand back a concise, sourced comparison: criteria and assumptions, options and
their best arguments, provisional conclusion, ADR impacts, migration costs, final
recommendation and remaining uncertainty. Cite repository files and external
evidence used. Exploration alone does not require an ADR.

Do not implement a disruptive alternative, change the architecture contract, or
change an ADR status without a human decision on adoption. If a replacement is
chosen for proposal, read `agent/decision-records.md` if installed; otherwise
follow the repository's ADR format. Draft `Proposed` ADRs, one per distinct
decision. Explain what remains in force if the proposals are
declined. A human changes and commits `Accepted`, `Rejected`, `Superseded`, or
`Deprecated` status. Use `/architect` for initial architecture and its full
document set.
----

# Solution exploration, pass 1: search choice

**Scope:** This is pass 1 only. I did not read any ADRs, decision logs or architecture docs, and I edited no files. The workspace holds only `problem.md` and the skill, so there is no code, current search setup or usage data to check. Every figure below is an engineering estimate and still needs measuring.

## 1. Outcome, constraints, criteria

**Outcome:** a search over about 5,000 local markdown notes that finds a note when the query uses different words from the text ("innkeeper" should find "tavern owner"), without losing what lexical search already does well.

**Hard constraints** (from `problem.md`):
- It must work offline.
- No campaign text may leave the device, and that includes sending it out to compute embeddings.
- Search may use at most 1.5 GB of memory, counted at peak and including indexing.
- No benchmark exists, so every quality and latency claim is unproven.

**Decision criteria:**

| # | Criterion | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| C1 | Recall on synonym and paraphrase queries | This is the reported problem |
| C2 | Precision on exact and invented terms (NPC names, place names, made-up words) | Campaign text is full of proper nouns that general models have never seen |
| C3 | Peak memory ≤ 1.5 GB, including the model, index and indexing spikes | Hard budget |
| C4 | Latency, both per query and for indexing and re-indexing after edits on a low-end laptop | Editors change notes all the time |
| C5 | Packaging: installer size, cross-platform native runtimes, model licence | It ships inside the app |
| C6 | Operating and maintenance cost: model upgrades, re-embedding, debugging | Long-term cost |
| C7 | Explainability: can users tell why a result matched? | Trust in an editor tool |
| C8 | Reversibility: can we back out cheaply if it doesn't pay off? | Nothing has been measured yet |

## 2. Options

Two options were dropped before comparison:
- **Cloud embeddings or hosted search** breaks the privacy and offline constraints.
- **Running a local LLM to rewrite queries** probably uses most or all of the 1.5 GB for a 1B+ parameter model, adds seconds of delay, and doesn't beat embeddings on recall.

### A. Keep the current lexical search
- **Best case:** it costs nothing, is predictable, and already handles exact names well (C2).
- **Problem:** it doesn't fix the reported synonym misses. It only makes sense as a control in a benchmark.

### B. Improve lexical retrieval
This means BM25 tuning, stemming and lemmatisation, field boosts (title, headings, tags, front-matter), fuzzy and typo matching, and query expansion. The expansion would use a general synonym list (WordNet-style) plus a campaign glossary: user- or app-maintained aliases such as "the Crimson King = Aldric".
- **Best case:**
  - It is cheap and deterministic.
  - It adds tens of MB at most, far under the budget.
  - It indexes almost instantly on edit and works on any laptop.
  - Users can see why a result matched (C7), and it is fully reversible.
  - A campaign glossary covers the invented names that general synonym lists and embedding models both miss (C2).
- **Costs and risks:**
  - It only finds synonyms someone has listed. It can't handle descriptive or paraphrase queries like "the scene where the party betrayed the guild".
  - General synonym expansion can hurt precision.
  - A hand-maintained glossary is ongoing work for users.
- **Unknown:** what share of the real misses are true paraphrases rather than spelling or word-form variants. Without that number, we can't tell whether B is enough on its own.

### C. The contributor's proposal: an in-process semantic index
The app would ship with a small embedding model and run it on the laptop through an embedded runtime. It would also embed a vector index (flat or HNSW) in the same process. There is no separate service.
- **Strongest case:**
  - It is the only option here that fixes the whole class of synonym and paraphrase misses, not a hand-listed subset (C1).
  - It meets both hard constraints by design: it works offline and no text leaves the device.
  - The corpus is small, which makes this unusually feasible. A rough sizing:
    - A small sentence-embedding model (MiniLM or bge-small class, 384 dimensions) is about 25–130 MB on disk, depending on quantisation.
    - The runtime peaks at roughly 150–400 MB.
    - 5,000 notes in about 10 chunks each gives ~50k vectors × 384 × 4 bytes ≈ 75 MB.
    - Even brute-force search over that many vectors runs in milliseconds.
    - The total is probably well under 1.5 GB, leaving room to spare (estimate, not measured).
  - Without a separate service there is no daemon, no port and no install step. The process boundary stays simple.
  - Keeping it in-process also preserves the local-first promise.
  - A full first-time index is plausibly minutes of CPU, and changes after that only re-embed edited chunks.
- **Costs:**
  - Installer gets bigger (model plus native runtime), and each OS and CPU architecture needs its own build.
  - The model licence must allow redistribution.
  - Re-indexing uses CPU and battery after imports.
  - Upgrading the model means re-embedding everything, so the index must store which model version built it.
  - Chunking needs design work.
  - Results are harder to explain to users (C7).
- **Risks:**
  - Pure vector search is known to do worse than lexical search on exact and rare tokens. Invented fantasy names are the worst case (C2), so swapping lexical out entirely could cause visible regressions.
  - Small models are mostly English. Non-English campaigns may get worse results.
  - Memory could spike past the budget if indexing batches are too large or someone later picks a bigger model. A 1024-dimension "large" model at fp32 alone is about 1.3 GB.
- **Unknowns:**
  - Real gain in quality on campaign text.
  - Latency on the slowest supported laptop.
  - How the runtime behaves on every target OS.
  - Whether users notice the extra CPU use.

### D. Hybrid: improved lexical (B) plus the in-process semantic index (C), with rank fusion
Both indexes run, and their result lists are merged (for example with reciprocal rank fusion). Lexical search stays the always-available fallback.
- **Best case:**
  - It gets C's paraphrase recall while B keeps exact-name precision, which removes C's main risk.
  - If the semantic model is missing or still indexing, search falls back to lexical, so users never see a regression.
  - It can sit behind a feature flag (C8).
  - The memory picture is the same as C, since lexical adds little.
- **Costs:**
  - Two indexes to keep in sync.
  - Fusion and score weights need tuning, which in turn needs the benchmark that doesn't exist yet.
  - It is somewhat more code than C alone.
- **Unknowns:** the same as C, plus how well the fusion weights carry over from one user's corpus to another's.

### E. A separate local service for semantic search
This could be a sidecar vector database or a local model server such as an Ollama-style runtime.
- **Best case:**
  - The ML runtime is isolated, so a crash or memory spike doesn't take down the editor.
  - It could be shared with other local AI features, and the model can be swapped independently.
- **Costs:**
  - An extra process to manage: lifecycle, ports, install, updates and support burden.
  - Memory is harder to keep within budget across two processes.
  - Some users will find a second local service at odds with a "local-first, just works" editor.
  - With 5,000 notes there is no scaling reason to split it out.
- **Verdict:** credible, but weaker than C or D unless crash isolation or sharing with other AI features is a real need.

## 3. Comparison

| | A Keep | B Better lexical | C In-process semantic | D Hybrid (B+C) | E Local service |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| C1 Synonym recall | ✗ | ◐ (listed synonyms only) | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| C2 Exact and invented names | ✓ | ✓ | ◐ (risk) | ✓ | ◐ |
| C3 Memory ≤ 1.5 GB | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ (est., small model) | ✓ (est.) | ◐ (two processes) |
| C4 Latency, re-index | ✓ | ✓ | ◐ (indexing CPU) | ◐ | ◐ |
| C5 Packaging | ✓ | ✓ | ◐ (native runtime, model) | ◐ | ✗ (extra install) |
| C6 Maintenance | ✓ | ✓ | ◐ (model versions) | ◐ (more) | ✗ |
| C7 Explainability | ✓ | ✓ | ◐ | ◐ | ◐ |
| C8 Reversibility | n/a | ✓ | ◐ | ✓ (flagged, lexical fallback) | ◐ |

## 4. Provisional recommendation

> **Provisional recommendation: D. Adopt the contributor's in-process semantic index, but as a hybrid on top of improved lexical search, and make adoption depend on a benchmark.**
>
> 1. **Build the benchmark first.** Assemble a test set of 100–200 real queries with known correct notes, drawn from real or representative campaigns. Include synonym, paraphrase, exact-name and misspelling cases. Measure recall@10 and nDCG, query p95 latency, indexing time and peak RSS on the slowest supported laptop.
> 2. **Ship the cheap lexical improvements (B) now.** That means stemming, field boosts, fuzzy matching and an alias/glossary mechanism. They help no matter what, and they are the baseline the semantic index must beat.
> 3. **Prototype the contributor's in-process index behind a feature flag.** Use a small quantised model, chunk-level vectors, a stored model-version field and incremental re-embedding. Merge results with lexical by rank fusion, and keep lexical as the fallback.
> 4. **Turn it on by default only if** it clearly beats B on synonym and paraphrase queries, does not regress exact-name queries, and stays within the memory and latency budgets with room to spare.
>
> Why D over C alone: the proposal's main weakness is invented proper nouns, and keeping lexical alongside removes that risk at little extra cost. Why D over B alone: B can't handle unlisted paraphrases, and this small corpus and 1.5 GB budget make on-device embeddings unusually cheap. Why not E: at this scale a separate service brings operating cost with no matching benefit.

## 5. Evidence that could change this

- **Switch to B alone** if the benchmark shows that improved lexical plus a glossary closes most of the gap, i.e. most misses are word-form variants or listed synonyms rather than true paraphrases.
- **Switch to C without fusion** if fusion adds complexity but the benchmark shows no exact-name regression for semantic-only search.
- **Delay or shrink the semantic part** if:
  - measured peak RSS or indexing time on low-end hardware gets near the budget,
  - battery or CPU complaints show up in testing, or
  - the native runtime is hard to package on a target platform.
- **Revisit model choice or the semantic part as a whole** if the campaigns are mostly non-English or heavy in invented language and small models do badly there.
- **Reconsider E** if crash isolation becomes a requirement, or other local AI features appear that would share a model runtime.
- **Reassess sizing** if the corpus is much bigger than 5,000 notes (for example, 50,000+).
- **Check in pass 2:** existing architecture decisions on in-process native dependencies, installer size limits, privacy and telemetry, or past rejections of ML features.

- **Reassess sizing** if the corpus is much bigger than 5,000 notes (for example, 50,000+).
- **Check in pass 2:** existing architecture decisions on in-process native dependencies, installer size limits, privacy and telemetry, or past rejections of ML features.
